planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; young plants grow slowly at first and tolerate more cold and clay soil than its coastal relative the pohutukawa.

directions: In the wild this tree famously begins life as a hemi-epiphyte, germinating high in the canopy of a host tree and sending roots down the host's trunk until it finally stands on its own, but in cultivation it grows as a conventional tree planted directly in the ground. It bears dense, dark olive-green leathery foliage and puts on a striking show of rust-red, bottlebrush-type flower clusters in early to mid-summer that are a major nectar source for native birds in New Zealand. It is slower growing and noticeably hardier to cold and wind than Metrosideros excelsa, tolerating heavier soils and some inland cold. Give it room to eventually become a large specimen tree, since old trees develop a massive trunk over many decades.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in sandy, excellently drained soil in full sun; coast tea tree is adapted to exposed dune sites and resents heavy, waterlogged ground.

directions: Masses of small, open, white five-petaled flowers cover the gray-green rounded leaves from late winter into spring, drawing bees and small insect-eating birds. In its native southeastern Australia it is one of the toughest sand-binding shrubs, forming dense thickets on exposed coastal dunes that withstand salt spray and wind. With age and pruning it can be trained into a small gnarled tree with attractive flaking bark, or sheared as a windbreak hedge. Avoid rich, moist soils, which encourage lank growth and shorten the plant's life.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; crush a leaf to confirm the strong lemon fragrance before buying, since seedling scent intensity can vary.

directions: The narrow, needle-like leaves release an intense lemon scent when brushed or crushed, a trait that has made this species popular for herbal tea, potpourri, and citral-rich essential oil production. Small white flowers appear in loose clusters in spring, followed by woody little seed capsules typical of the genus. It is a fast-growing large shrub or small tree, useful as an informal aromatic screen, and responds well to a hard prune after flowering to keep it dense and encourage fresh fragrant growth. Good drainage is essential, as with other tea trees.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in average to moist soil; this riparian species tolerates both periodic flooding and, once established, considerable drought.

directions: Native to riverbanks across northern and eastern Australia, this fine-textured, weeping-branched shrub bears small cream flower spikes that are pleasant but not showy, so it is grown chiefly for its dense, finely divided foliage and graceful arching habit. Golden-leaved selections sold in nurseries bring bright color to hedges and screens, while the plain green form is valued for erosion control along waterways and as a fast, wind-tolerant windbreak. The papery, fibrous bark typical of melaleucas adds winter interest. It responds well to shearing and can be kept as a dense low hedge or allowed to grow into a small specimen tree.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in full sun to light shade; this species tolerates wet, compacted, and saline soils better than most melaleucas, making it useful in difficult sites.

directions: Creamy-white bottlebrush flower spikes appear mainly in summer and are attractive to bees and honeyeaters, while the small, stiff, pointed leaves that give the tree its common name provide a prickly, fine-textured canopy. The thick, spongy, multi-layered papery bark is a standout ornamental feature year-round and offers useful insulation from fire and frost. It tolerates boggy, compacted, and brackish soils better than most of its relatives, which has made it a popular street and park tree in warm climates. Prune only to shape when young, since mature trees develop an attractive gnarled trunk best left undisturbed.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; like other Western Australian hakeas it demands sharp drainage and no phosphorus fertilizer.

directions: Tall, tapering spikes of vivid orange-red flowers up to 10 inches long line the older wood from late winter into spring, held above fine, needle-like bright green leaves that let the blooms show clearly through the airy canopy. The long-lasting flower spikes make excellent cut flowers and are a strong draw for nectar-feeding birds. This upright shrub needs full sun for the best flowering and, like its Proteaceae relatives, demands lean, extremely well-drained soil free of phosphorus-rich fertilizer. It can tolerate light shade but blooms far less heavily there.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in a sheltered, sunny spot with sharp drainage; this kowhai resents soggy winter soil and benefits from protection from strong wind while young.

directions: This species is distinguished from the closely related South Island kowhai by noticeably larger, more widely spaced leaflets and bigger, more vividly golden flowers, which it often produces at a younger age and in heavier bloom. The pendulous spring flower clusters are a major nectar source for native birds such as tui and bellbird in New Zealand gardens, and seed pods that follow are winged and papery. It forms an open, rounded-headed small tree that can be trained to a single trunk or espaliered against a warm wall in cooler climates. Water regularly while establishing, then taper off, since mature trees are drought tolerant and dislike wet feet.
sources: University of Auckland New Zealand Plants
